note: This is the alpha-equivalence of bound variables. The proof assistant handles it. It is not a statement.

quote: yielding $e(\blank)$ as alternative notation for the function $x \mapsto e(x)$.
note: This is the underscore notation for anonymous functions. It is only notation.

quote: The notation $b \jdeq c$ will denote the statement that the expressions $b$ and $c$ become the same thing …
note: This is the meta-level definitional equality (and \defeq for definitions). It corresponds to the judgmental equality of Narya. It is not an internal statement.

quote: We define the \emph{composite} function $g \circ f : X \to Z$ by setting $g \circ f \defeq (a \mapsto g(f(a)))$.

note: Narya has one Type : Type. The formalization models a universe as a small-predicate with closure fields. It also has nested pairs U : U' with cumulativity. There is no hierarchy U_0 : U_1 : … and no designated smallest U_0.

quote: It follows from the properties above that there are an infinite number of universes, for each one is an element of a larger one.
note: This is a metatheoretic claim about the ambient hierarchy. Narya has Type : Type (total_universe contains its own type). Thus a faithful statement of the claim is not possible.

quote: The flexibility offered by this correspondence between families of types in $\UU$ and functions to $\UU$ will often be used.

quote: Here are Peano's rules for constructing the natural numbers in the form that is used in type theory.

quote: that different natural numbers have different successors; and that no number has $0$ as its successor. Those omitted rules remain true

note: The lemma adjunction_transposition gives the BookEquiv Hom_D(F c, d) ≃ Hom_C(c, G d) whose map is α_{c,d}.

quote: There is however another way of packaging this information. We can transpose the identity $\id_{F(C)}$ to get an arrow $\eta_C : C \to_{\mathcal C} GF(C)$, and the identity $\id_{G(D)}$ to get an arrow $\varepsilon_D : FG(D) \to_{\mathcal D} D$.
note: The unit is η_c = α(id_{F c}) and the counit is ε_d = α⁻¹(id_{G d}) (core module 603). Here α⁻¹ is the section that the isomorphism data supply. The lemma adjunction_counit_transpose gives α(ε_d) = id_{G d}.

note: The margin figure shows the two triangles (quoted here in formula form). They are proved for every wild adjunction in xca:adj-triangles.

quote: Conversely, given $F$, $G$, $\eta$, and $\varepsilon$, along with fillers for the triangle laws, we can recover $\alpha$ by sending $f : F(C) \to_{\mathcal D} D$ to the composite $C \xrightarrow{\eta_C} GF(C) \xrightarrow{G(f)} G(D)$.
note: The construction adjunction_from_triangles uses exactly α(f) = G(f) ∘ η_c. For an adjunction, adjunction_transpose_via_unit shows α(f) = G(f) ∘ η_c. Thus α is recovered from its own unit (adjunction_round_trip_transpose).

note: The formalization gives maps in both directions between RightAdjointData and UnitCounitAdjunction. The round trips return α, η and ε up to pointwise identifications, with the same G on the nose. An equivalence of the two types of bundles is not proved. It would need coherence of the wild identifications.

quote: We shall see later in~\cref{cor:adj-unique} for a functor whose domain is a category, that the data of a right adjoint is a proposition.
note: This is a forward reference to cor:adj-unique. The lemma right_adjoints_agree shows that any two right adjoints of F have identified right functors.

quote: One benefit of the Yoneda lemma is that we can characterize adjoint functors in terms of representability, and then derive the uniqueness of adjoint functors in the case of categories.
note: The lemma right_adjoint_data_representations_equiv gives RightAdjointData (C .wild) D F ≃ (d : D) → Σ x, Hom_D(F -, d) ≅ h_x (via lem:adj-via-repr). Uniqueness for categories is right_adjoint_data_prop.

quote: From cor:adj-unique we immediately see the following:
note: The formalization derives lem:cat-equiv-is-prop from cor:adj-unique (right_adjoint_data_prop, module 624). It also uses that the unit and counit isomorphism conditions are propositions. An independent proof is is_cat_equivalence_prop.

quote: It's often useful to show that a functor F : C → D is an equivalence by giving just a functor G : D → C along with natural isomorphisms η : id_C ≅ GF and ε : FG ≅ id_D. This is analogous to lem:weq-iso, and we refer to AKS2015 Lemma 6.2 for the implementation.

quote: We again refer to AKS2015 Lemma 6.6 for details.
note: This is a bibliographic pointer. The lemma itself is fully formalized (cat_equivalence_ff_split_eso_equiv).

quote: From this we conclude that if C is category, then split essential surjectivity is equivalent to essential surjectivity, and then lem:equiv-precat-is-ff-split-eso gives one of the fundamental theorems of category theory
note: The lemma split_eso_eso_equiv says this: for a category C and a fully faithful F, IsSplitEso ≃ IsEso (BookEquiv). Together with lem:equiv-precat-is-ff-split-eso, this gives thm:ff-eso-equiv.

quote: Compare lem:inj+surj, stating that a function f : A → B of types is an equivalence if and only if it is injective and surjective.
note: This is a cross-reference to chapter 2. There, lem:inj+surj is embedding_surjection_equiv (module 12). The categorical analogue is the injectivity/image description of thm:ff-eso-equiv.

quote: There is also a version of this statement for precategories, but it concerns the stronger notion of isomorphism of precategories, i.e. fully faithful functors that induce an equivalence on the types of objects. The point is that for categories, this is the same as equivalence.
note: The lemma precategory_path_equiv says this: for precategories, the map (C = D) → PrecatIsomorphism C D is a BookEquiv. This map is defined by path induction (refl ↦ identity functor). The proof uses a structure identity principle. This principle contracts the object type, the hom family, the identities and the composition by univalence and function extensionality. The lemma precat_iso_cat_equivalence_equiv says that, for categories, isomorphisms of precategories are equivalent to equivalences.

quote: Since the type of functors between categories is 1-truncated, we conclude as well:
note: The lemma functor_type_groupoid says that WildFunctor C (D .wild) is a groupoid when D is a category. C is arbitrary.

quote: This result is one of the reasons that the primary objects of interest in category theory are the categories (i.e. univalent precategories), rather than the more general precategories.
note: This is a motivational remark without mathematical content.

quote: However, it's occasionally useful to present a category via a non-univalent precategory. This will not be equivalent to the corresponding category, so we need a notion that establishes their connection.
note: The literal reading ('will not be equivalent') can fail. The indiscrete precategory on Bool is not univalent, but it is equivalent to the terminal category. The intended reading is 'need not be equivalent', that is, a weak equivalence need not be an equivalence. A counterexample to that needs the failure of a choice principle. Thus it is not provable here (it is consistent with choice).

quote: From the point of view of categories, however, weak equivalences are as good as equivalences.
note: The result lem:precomp-equiv-cat (precomposition_cat_equivalence) makes this precise. For domains that are categories, thm:ff-eso-equiv also makes it precise.

quote: Our goal now is to construct for every precategory C a category L(C) along with a weak equivalence η : C → L(C). Here, L(C) is called the Rezk completion of C.
note: This is formalized in module 673.

quote: The idea is a generalization of the Cayley's lem:allgpsarepermutationgps, which is also how we'll go from abstract groups to concrete groups in ch:absgroup.
note: This is reading guidance and a forward reference. It makes no mathematical claim.

note: Set is SetCat, the category of all sets of Narya's single universe (the book's Set_U). The presheaf category is a category by functor_wild_univalent (module 621) (xca:functor-cat-univalent).

note: This is cor:yo-ff from module 622. The formalization uses it for rezk_unit_ff.

note: The lemma rezk_unit_ff is literally yoneda_fully_faithful, because the hom-sets of the full subcategory are those of Set^{C^op}. The lemma rezk_unit_eso returns the membership proof of the object.

quote: Suppose now that $\mathcal C$ is essentially $\UU$-small, meaning that the type of objects $\Ob(\mathcal C)$ and all hom-sets are essentially $\UU$-small.
note: In the smallness-predicate model, this is equivalent to IsSmallWildPrecat of rem:cat-sizes (module 606). In that model, essential smallness and smallness agree.

quote: Then we have the hom-functor $\hom_{\mathcal C} : \mathcal C\op \times \mathcal C \to \Set_\UU$, so we get a Yoneda embedding $\mathcal C \to \Set_\UU^{\mathcal C\op}$.
note: Narya has one universe, so the presheaf category is valued in all sets. We record that the representable presheaves take U-small values when C is locally U-small. The two-variable hom-functor on C^op × C is not defined separately.

quote: Since $\Ob(\mathcal C)$ is essentially $\UU$-small, then $\Set_\UU^{\mathcal C\op}$ is locally $\UU$-small, and hence so is $L(\mathcal C)$.
note: The lemma presheaf_hom_essentially_small says this. Let C be essentially U-small. Then the natural transformations between presheaves on C with U-small values form an essentially U-small type. This is the statement that the book's Set_U^{C^op} is locally U-small. Via Yoneda, L(C) is locally U-small even without a smallness hypothesis on Ob(C).

quote: And now $\Ob(L(\mathcal C))$ is the image of $\Ob(\yo) : \Ob(\mathcal C) \to \Ob(\Set_\UU^{\mathcal C\op})$, which is then essentially $\UU$-small by the Replacement~\cref{pri:replacement}.
note: The lemma rezk_objects_image_equiv gives Ob(L(C)) ≃ Image(Ob(yo)). By the univalence of Set^{C^op}, mere isomorphisms are mere identifications. Our Ob(Set^{C^op}) is not locally U-small. Thus Replacement is applied to the surjection Ob(η) : Ob(C) → Ob(L(C)). Its codomain is locally U-small, because it is univalent with U-small hom-sets.

quote: even though $\Set_\UU^{\mathcal C\op}$ is only locally $\UU$-small when $\mathcal C$ is essentially $\UU$-small
note: The 'only when' direction is a cited theorem of Freyd and Street: if Set_U^{C^op} is locally small, then C is essentially small. It is not formalized. The 'when' direction is presheaf_hom_essentially_small.

quote: Another consequence of~\cref{cor:Cat-ua} is the following.
note: This is about the organisation of the proof. Our proof of the second part of thm:1types-are-groupoids uses the identity of (pre)categories (precategory_path_equiv, category_path_precat_equiv). The first part needs only path induction.

quote: [A,B] \jdeq \sum_{f : A \to B} \sum_{g : \prod_{x,y:A}(x\eqto y) \to (f(x) \eqto f(y))} \biggl(\prod_{x:A} g(\refl x) = \refl{f(x)}\biggr) \times \biggl(\prod_{x,y,z:A}\prod_{p:x\eqto y}\prod_{q:y\eqto z} g(qp) = g(q)g(p)\biggr)
note: The formalization gives an equivalence whose round trips are reflexivities (eta for records), in place of the judgmental equality. In PathWild, qp is p · q.

quote: Here, the two bracketed components are propositions.
note: This requires B to be a 1-type. Then the hom-sets of the path groupoid of B are sets.

quote: By path induction, $g$ is determined by its action on reflexivity, so the first bracketed component nails it down, so only the first component, the function $f:A\to B$, remains up to equivalence.
note: The lemma path_family_refl_equiv gives (Π x y, (x = y) → P x y) ≃ Π x, P x x by evaluation at refl. The lemma path_functor_action_contractible says that the pairs (g, identity law) are contractible with the centre ap f. The lemma path_groupoid_functors_equiv gives [A, B] ≃ (A → B).

This functor is fully faithful because it is ap of an equivalence. Thus it is an equivalence by thm:ff-eso-equiv. The parenthetical remark is informal.

quote: This shows that $\UU^{\le 1} \to \Gpd$ is injective, so by~\cref{lem:inj+surj}, it remains to show it is surjective.
note: We construct the inverse G ↦ Ob(G) directly. Then we derive injectivity and surjectivity from the resulting equivalence. We do not go in the reverse direction.

quote: Observe that for a groupoid, the hom-sets and the identity arrows are determined by the univalence condition.
note: In a groupoid, (x = y) ≃ (x ≅ y) ≃ hom(x, y), and idtoiso(refl) = id. The map that forgets invertibility is an equivalence, because isIso is a contractible proposition.

quote: And relative to this, the composition operation is determined (by path induction) by its values at $\refl{y}p$, for all $p:x\eqto y$. But these values are forced to be $p$ by the left unit law.
note: The lemma cat_idtoiso_concat (module 626) proves idtoiso(p · q) = idtoiso(q) ∘ idtoiso(p). The proof is by path induction on q and uses the left unit law. This lemma is the composition law of the comparison functor.

quote: This identifies any groupoid with the path groupoid on its objects, showing that $\UU^{\le 1} \to \Gpd$ is surjective.
note: The formalization gives an isomorphism of precategories from the path groupoid of Ob(G) to G. It turns this isomorphism into an identification in Gpd via precategory_path_equiv (module 645).

quote: Can we think of them just in terms of categories? It turns out we can.
note: This is motivation. The precise content is thm:flagged-cat-equiv.

quote: The idea is that any precategory $\mathcal C$ presents a category $L(\mathcal C)$, its Rezk completion, but it has more structure, namely its type of objects, $\Ob(\mathcal C)$, as well as the relation between these and those of $L(\mathcal C)$, given by the functor $\eta : \mathcal C \to L(\mathcal C)$.
note: The structure is packaged as rezk_flag C = (L(C), Ob(C), Ob(η), surjectivity).

quote: Since $\eta$ is fully faithful, this structure boils down to the map on objects, $\Ob(\eta) : \Ob(\mathcal C) \to \Ob(L(\mathcal C))$.
note: C is recovered (up to identification of precategories) as the pullback of L(C) along Ob(η).

quote: The terminology is a bit whimsical: it's meant to indicate that we have a fat ``flag'' object, the category $\mathcal C$, equipped with a thinner ``flagpole'' object, the (higher) groupoid $A$, connected by the function $f$
note: This is an explanation of terminology with a picture.

quote: The flagged categories describe the fibers of the Rezk completion.
note: The fibre of L : Precat → Category at D is equivalent to FlagStructure D.

quote: We conclude that the following triangle commutes definitionally, displaying the fiber of Rezk completion at a category $\mathcal C$ as the type $\sum_{A:\UU}\sum_{f:A\to\Ob(\mathcal C)}\issurj(f)$
note: The equation fst ∘ F = L holds by refl. The fibre statement uses that F is an equivalence. It contracts the path component of the fibre of fst.

quote: The inverse at a triple $(\mathcal C,A,f)$ ``pulls back'' the (pre)category structure $\mathcal C$ along $f$ to get a precategory $\mathcal A$ on the object type $A$ and $\hom(x,y) \defeq \hom_{\mathcal C}(f(x), f(y))$, and likewise using $f$ to define identity arrows, composition, as well as unit and associativity laws.
note: Litmus tests: the pullback along the identity of Ob(D) gives D by refl. The pullback of Set along ★ ↦ Bool gives the endomaps of Bool.

quote: By construction, this extends $f$ to a fully faithful functor $f : \mathcal A \to \mathcal C$.
note: The functor is f on objects and the identity on arrows.

quote: This is also essentially surjective by the surjectivity of $f$, hence inducing an equivalence $L(\mathcal A) \equivto \mathcal C$.
note: Let F : C → D be a weak equivalence into a category. Then the restricted Yoneda functor d ↦ hom_D(F -, d) is an equivalence D ≃ L(C) that sends F(c) to η(c) (module 674). This gives the identification D = L(A) that flagged_round_trip uses.

quote: For the other round trip, starting with a precategory $\mathcal C$, we use the fully faithfulness of $\eta : \mathcal C \to L(\mathcal C)$ to identify the precategory structure on $\Ob(\mathcal C)$ with that pulled back from $L(\mathcal C)$.
note: The functor that is the identity on objects and yo on arrows is an isomorphism of precategories C ≅ Ob(η)*L(C). Thus it gives an identification (module 645).

quote: We have also seen two instances of limits and colimits, namely terminal and initial objects
note: The book does not define general limits and colimits. The section treats only products, coproducts and pullbacks. Thus the claim has no formal content here.

quote: We immediately recognize the product of types $A\times B$, along with the first and second projections, as a product cone $(A\times B,\fst,snd)$ in the wild category of types.
note: The factorizations of a cone (X, x₁, x₂) through A × B form a retract of a based path space. Thus they are contractible.

quote: Likewise, in the category of groups, the product G×H from ex:productofgroups forms a product cone when equipped with the projection homomorphisms.
note: The formalization proves IsProductCone (GroupCat .wild) G H (product_group G H, (product_group_proj1, product_group_proj2)) in the sense of def:prod-in-a-cat (module 665). The map f ↦ (p1 ∘ f, p2 ∘ f) : Hom(K, G × H) → Hom(K, G) × Hom(K, H) is an equivalence. Its inverse pairs the classifying maps and the pointing paths. The factorizations of a cone are its book fiber. Hence GroupCat has binary products. By univalence, every product cone on G, H equals this one. Litmus test: the cone (Σ_3, id, id) factors through the diagonal x ↦ (x, x) (refl).

quote: We say that a (wild) category \emph{has binary products} if every pair of objects $A,B$ as a product cone.
note: HasBinaryProducts C ≔ (a b : C .ob) → ProductCone C a b. For a univalent C, it is a proposition. The word 'as' in the book is a typo for 'has'.

quote: In this case we are justified by~\cref{xca:product-cone-prop} in writing $(A\times B,\fst,\snd)$ for the (unique) product cone on $A,B$.
note: In a univalent wild precategory, a given product cone makes the type of product cones contractible. In the wild category of types, every product cone equals (A × B, fst, snd).

quote: Like every categorical notion, there is of course a dual notion, obtained by turning all the arrows around.
note: The relation to products is as follows. IsCoproductCocone C a b K is by refl IsProductCone (OppositeWild C) a b K. The cocone precategory is the opposite of the cone precategory of C^op.

quote: In other words, a coproduct cocone is an initial cocone under the pair of objects $A,B$.
note: For C with hom-sets, this holds by refl. IsCoproductCocone C a b K is the statement that every hom type out of K in the cocone precategory is contractible. This is def:initial-obj, unfolded.

quote: In the wild category of types, we have the coproduct cocones $(A \coprod B, \inl{}, \inr{})$.
note: Precomposition with inl, inr is an equivalence (A ⊔ B → X) ≃ (A → X) × (B → X). The factorizations of a cocone are a retract of its book fiber.

quote: We haven't yet seen the coproduct of groups; knowing about products and categorical duality, we'd be bound to discover them! We shall study them in sec:coprod.
note: This is a forward reference without a claim that can be checked. The book constructs and studies the coproduct of groups in sec:coprod (chapter 8, congp.tex, module range 800–899). It needs pushouts of classifying types, and chapter 6 does not provide them. The coproduct cocones of types in the same sentence belong to def:coprod-in-a-cat (module 665).

quote: Let's look at another pair of examples: pullbacks and pushouts.
note: This chapter does not define pushouts. Module 666 formalizes pullbacks of types.

quote: the ``pullback'' which we will now define should be thought about as the type of all pairs of elements $(b,c):B\times C$ so that $f(b)\eqto g(c)$.
note: This agrees with def:pullback: TypePullback B C D f g ≔ Σ_{(b,c)} f(b) = g(c).

quote: This construction is important in many situations also beyond group theory.
note: This is motivation.

quote: In view of \cref{xca:univpropofpullback} we will say that we have a \emph{pullback diagram} [...] to indicate that we have an element in $(A\to B)\times_{(A\to D)}(A\to C)$ such that the resulting map $A\to B\times_DC$ is an equivalence.
note: IsPullbackSquare A B C D f g w ≔ BookIsEquiv of the gap map a ↦ (β(a), γ(a), happly p a). As checks, the formalization shows that the defining square of B ×_D C and the preimage square of the example are pullback diagrams.

quote: This is emphasized with the little $\lrcorner$ symbol in the upper left corner.
note: This is diagram notation.

quote: \section{Monoidal categories}
note: The section is empty in the pinned book. Only LaTeX comments follow. There is nothing to formalize.

quote: In this chapter we will implement an inverse construction, how to obtain a (concrete) group from an abstract one
note: The construction concr (module 707) is the group that the abstract torsors classify. Module 709 proves both round trips. Thus abstr : Group → AbstractGroup is an equivalence with inverse concr.

quote: we show how to obtain a (concrete) homomorphism from an abstract one
note: The function deloop_hom (module 710) reconstructs a homomorphism G → H from an abstract homomorphism abstr G → abstr H (lem:homomabstrconcr). The function concr_hom (module 742) is concr on morphisms.

quote: Of course this is not a reason to stop here, but to continue finding out which parts of group theory benefit from the concrete approach.
note: This footnote gives motivation. It contains no mathematical claim.

quote: More precisely, we give an equivalence of categories between the categories of concrete and of abstract groups.
note: This is thm:concr-equiv-cats, module 744, with the wild precategories GroupWild (chapter 6) and AbstractGroupWild.

quote: One could advocate for the name `abstract monoid' here, were it not the case that we have no concrete analogue for monoids in our setting. The reason is the symmetry of the identity types.
note: This footnote is about terminology. The reason that it gives is informal: identity types are symmetric, so loop spaces are groups.

quote: A monoid is a collection of data consisting only of \ref{struc:under-set}, \ref{struc:unit}, and \ref{struc:mult-op} from the list in \cref{def:abstractgroup}. In other words, the existence of inverses is not assumed.

Examples of monoids without inverses are list_monoid_no_inverse (module 720) and two_element_monoid_no_inverse (module 728).

UnitLaws(S,e,μ) :≡ ..., AssocLaw(S,μ) :≡ ..., MonoidLaws(S,e,μ) :≡ isSet(S) × UnitLaws × AssocLaw, InverseLaw(S,e,μ,ι) :≡ ..., GroupLaws(S,e,μ,ι) :≡ MonoidLaws × InverseLaw
note: Module 700 defines the named laws as displayed (products nested to the right). They are propositions: monoid_laws_prop and group_laws_prop (isSet S is part of MonoidLaws), and inverse_law_prop (module 721). The equivalence group_laws_equiv identifies GroupLaws with the laws record of module 403.

quote: an abstract group $\mathscr G$ will be a quintuple of the form $\mathscr G \jdeq (S,e,\mu,\iota,!)$. For brevity, we will usually omit the proof of the properties from the display, since it's unique, and write an abstract group as though it were a quadruple
note: The quintuple form is AbstractGroupSigma. It is equivalent to the record AbstractGroup, with refl round trips (abstract_group_sigma_equiv). The uniqueness of the proof of the laws is group_laws_prop / abstract_group_laws_prop. The lemmas abstract_group_laws_irrelevant (module 430) and abstract_group_path_of_data (module 702) show that the quadruple (S, e, μ, ι) determines the abstract group.

note: This is a section overview without a mathematical claim. The notion is IsAbstractHom / AbstractHom (module 403), and the exercise is xca:onlymult-hom.

quote: Thus we see that, due to the properties of the abstract groups, if $f$ preserves multiplication, then $f$ also preserves unit and inverses.
note: This is xca:onlymult-hom (module 701). The lemma abstract_hom_monoid_hom packages the unit equation into a monoid homomorphism.

note: Module 728: M is Bool with 0 = false, 1 = true, x·y = x ∧ y and unit true (two_element_monoid). The trivial monoid is unit_monoid on Unit. The map h = monoid_footnote_map (constant false) preserves multiplication by refl. The formalization refutes h(*) = 1. Thus h is not a MonoidHom, and the monoid analogue of xca:onlymult-hom fails (monoid_mul_preserving_not_unit_preserving).

note: An inverse x of 0 gives 0 = 0·x = 1 (two_element_monoid_zero_inverse, whose conclusion is Id Bool false true). Thus M has no inverse operation with the law of inverses, and not even mere inverses. No abstract group has M as its underlying monoid (two_element_monoid_not_abstract_group, module 728).

quote: it will then be relatively simple to show that the constructions of forming the abstract group of a group and taking the group classified by the torsors of an abstract group are inverse to each other.
note: Module 709.

quote: Then we can view $X$ as the classifying function of a group homomorphism from $G$ to $\SG_{X(\sh_G)}$.
note: Chapter 5 (rem:GSet=SetHomG, module 560) gives GSet G ≃ Σ_S GroupActionOnSet G S with GroupActionOnSet G S = GroupHom G (permutation_group S). The restriction of the codomain to the component is ptd_conn_to_comp_equiv.

note: The principal abstr(G)-torsor acts by g · h = concat h g (left multiplication / postcomposition with g), by refl (agset_principal_abstr_act). For z ≡ sh_G, the abstr(G)-set of ex:BqG is the principal torsor (bq_gset_principal).

note: Module 712 gives the abstr(G)-set (sh_G = z, r ↦ r g⁻¹) and its identification with the principal torsor at z ≡ sh_G (through xca:absprtorsor).

quote: Clearly, the types $\absGSet$ and $\absGTor$ are groupoids, and the latter is by definition connected.
